title: Clustering and Token Denoising for Faster and More Robust VLMs
summary: Recent Visual-Language Models (VLMs) have enhanced the capabilities of pre-trained LLMs by adding vision tokens alongside text, with approaches like LLaVA showing impressive results. However, the computational burden of processing up to 576 or 729 visual tokens makes edge deployment challenging. While various token pruning techniques require retraining, some are training-free and thus can easily adapt to architecture changes. We introduce ClustRS, a two-part, training-free algorithm for robust token pruning. Its first component is an attention-weighted, clustering algorithm that selects representative tokens from each semantic cluster. The second component, Residual Shrinkage, is a one-pass denoising step on the selected tokens. These training-free lightweight steps make LLaVA ready for real-world data, improving robustness to a wide range of image-noise types and intensities. Experimental results on the ScienceQA-IMG and MM-VET benchmarks show our method outperforms attention- and diversity-based methods by up to 20\% under extreme noise and token conditions (reducing tokens by 97\%, down to 16 tokens) on LLaVA 1.5 7b and achieves exceptional results on LLaVA-OneVision, where we match baseline performance with fewer than one-third of their tokens under mild noise conditions. Our study demonstrates a simple yet powerful alternative to both score-only and diversity-only pruning rules, paving the way for compute-efficient and noise-resilient VLM deployment.

AI.tldr: ClustRS is a training-free, two-part token pruning algorithm for Visual-Language Models that combines attention-weighted clustering with Residual Shrinkage denoising to reduce visual tokens (up to 97%) while improving robustness to image noise, outperforming existing attention- and diversity-based methods on ScienceQA-IMG and MM-VET benchmarks.
AI.motivation: VLMs like LLaVA add up to 576-729 visual tokens, making edge deployment computationally expensive. Existing token pruning methods either require retraining or fail to handle noisy real-world data effectively.
AI.method: ClustRS consists of two training-free components: (1) an attention-weighted clustering algorithm that selects representative tokens from each semantic cluster, and (2) Residual Shrinkage, a one-pass denoising step applied to the selected tokens.
AI.result: Outperforms attention- and diversity-based methods by up to 20% under extreme noise and token conditions (reducing tokens by 97% down to 16 tokens) on LLaVA 1.5 7b, and matches baseline performance with fewer than one-third of tokens under mild noise on LLaVA-OneVision.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that combining clustering (diversity) with attention weighting and denoising provides a simple yet powerful alternative to score-only or diversity-only pruning rules, enabling compute-efficient and noise-resilient VLM deployment.

title: SceneGTMM: A Conformal Mapping-based Scene-Aware Transferable GNN-Transformer Dual-Graph Interaction Framework for Map Matching
summary: Map matching is a key technology connecting positioning data with high precision road networks, but it faces challenges in noise robustness, cross regional transfer, and interpretability. To addr ess the limitations of existing methods in local global fusion, dynamic road network adaptation, and reliance on black box mod els, this paper proposes SceneGTMM, a transferable GNN Transformer dual graph interaction map matching framework based on a conformal mapping based scene relative strategy. 1) Conformal mapping based scene relative strategy: constructs trajectory centric local coordinate systems to reduce dependence on the training road network, supporting cross regional transfer and dynamic road network updates; 2) GNN Transformer dual graph interaction architecture: a GNN modeled road graph captures local topological constraints, while a Transformer modeled trajectory graph captures global temporal dependencies, and cross graph attention achieves noise suppression and semantic alignment; 3) CRF enhanced structured prediction: combines the global context of the Transformer with the topological transition constraints of CRF to improve path connectivity and robustness. Experiments show that SceneGTM achieves over 80% accuracy on multi source trajectories with positioning errors of 16 50 meters, representing a 5.3% improvement over HMM. In cross city transfer scenarios, it outperforms MTrajRec, GraphMM, and TMM, and enhances interpretability through attention and relative coordinate visualization. This study provides a new paradigm for high precision, transferable map matching for real time traffic perception and autonomous driving path planning.

AI.tldr: SceneGTMM is a transferable map matching framework combining a conformal mapping-based scene-relative strategy, a GNN-Transformer dual-graph interaction architecture, and CRF-enhanced structured prediction. It achieves over 80% accuracy on multi-source trajectories with positioning errors of 16-50m, outperforming HMM by 5.3% and surpassing existing methods in cross-city transfer scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing map matching methods face challenges in noise robustness, cross-regional transferability, and interpretability. Limitations include poor local-global fusion, inability to adapt to dynamic road networks, and reliance on black-box models.
AI.method: 1) A conformal mapping-based scene-relative strategy constructs trajectory-centric local coordinate systems to reduce dependence on the training road network; 2) A GNN-Transformer dual-graph interaction architecture where a GNN-modeled road graph captures local topological constraints and a Transformer-modeled trajectory graph captures global temporal dependencies, with cross-graph attention for noise suppression and semantic alignment; 3) CRF-enhanced structured prediction combining Transformer global context with CRF topological transition constraints for improved path connectivity and robustness.
AI.result: SceneGTMM achieves over 80% accuracy on multi-source trajectories with positioning errors of 16-50 meters, representing a 5.3% improvement over HMM. In cross-city transfer scenarios, it outperforms MTrajRec, GraphMM, and TMM, and enhances interpretability through attention and relative coordinate visualization.
AI.conclusion: This study provides a new paradigm for high-precision, transferable map matching, with implications for real-time traffic perception and autonomous driving path planning.

title: Does Marginal Coverage Guarantee Class-Conditional Safety for Zero-Shot VLMs Under Shift?
comment: Accepted at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Uncertainty Quantification for Computer Vision (UNCV). 34 pages (16 main + 18 supplementary), 10 figures
summary: Split-conformal prediction provides marginal coverage under exchangeability and is increasingly used as an abstention layer for zero-shot vision-language models (VLMs). We audit this practice under deployment shift for CLIP, OpenCLIP, and SigLIP across ImageNet and non-ImageNet settings. Marginal coverage can remain relatively high while class-conditional tail coverage collapses: on ImageNet-Sketch, worst-class coverage falls to $\approx 0$ and 10-12% of classes lie below a finite-sample null floor, despite marginal coverage of about 0.86. The failure is aligned with target-domain class accuracy but is not predicted by the source-domain diagnostics we test. Source-side Mondrian calibration improves the in-distribution tail but does not transfer, while clustered conformal and Conf-OT improve marginal or average metrics without recovering the worst-class tail. Target-side class calibration substantially lifts the tail, but requires labels for every class and remains set-size-intensive. We further identify a 2-3$\times$ cross-family efficiency gap and show that native SigLIP sigmoid scores remove APS's probability-mass interpretation. The findings persist across the tested model scale, pretraining corpus, prompt, miscoverage level $α$, and shifted non-ImageNet settings. Marginal conformal coverage should therefore be treated as an average reliability statistic, not as a safety guarantee for the class tail.

AI.tldr: This paper audits split-conformal prediction as an abstention layer for zero-shot VLMs under deployment shift, finding that marginal coverage remains high while worst-class tail coverage collapses to near zero on shifted datasets like ImageNet-Sketch. Source-side calibration methods fail to transfer, target-side calibration helps but requires full labels, and the authors advocate treating marginal coverage as an average reliability statistic rather than a safety guarantee.
AI.motivation: Split-conformal prediction is increasingly used as an abstention layer for zero-shot vision-language models (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP), providing marginal coverage guarantees under exchangeability. However, deployment shift can violate these assumptions, and the safety implications for the class tail remain underexplored. The paper aims to audit whether conformal coverage guarantees hold meaningfully under realistic distribution shifts.
AI.method: The authors empirically audit conformal prediction under deployment shift across CLIP, OpenCLIP, and SigLIP on ImageNet and non-ImageNet settings. They measure marginal coverage, class-conditional tail coverage, and evaluate multiple calibration approaches: source-side Mondrian calibration, clustered conformal prediction, Conf-OT, and target-side class calibration. They also analyze cross-family efficiency gaps and the APS probability-mass interpretation with SigLIP sigmoid scores.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Worst-class coverage collapses to ~0 on ImageNet-Sketch with 10-12% of classes below a finite-sample null floor despite ~0.86 marginal coverage. (2) Tail failure aligns with target-domain class accuracy but is not predicted by source-domain diagnostics. (3) Source-side Mondrian calibration improves in-distribution tail but does not transfer. (4) Clustered conformal and Conf-OT improve marginal/average metrics without recovering the worst-class tail. (5) Only target-side class calibration lifts the tail, but requires labels for every class. (6) A 2-3x cross-family efficiency gap exists, and SigLIP sigmoid scores break APS's probability-mass interpretation. Findings persist across scale, corpus, prompt, miscoverage level, and non-ImageNet shifts.
AI.conclusion: Marginal conformal coverage should be treated as an average reliability statistic, not as a safety guarantee for the class tail. The paper highlights that current conformal calibration methods are insufficient for safe deployment under shift, and only label-intensive target-side calibration can meaningfully recover tail coverage.

title: CAViAR: A Causal Video Dataset for Fine-Grained Accident Reasoning in Real-World Scenarios
summary: While modern autonomous driving systems excel at perception tasks such as object detection and trajectory prediction, they lack the high-level causal reasoning required to interpret traffic accidents. In particular, determining responsibility, such as identifying who is at fault and which traffic rule was violated, remains largely unexplored in current benchmarks. To this end, we introduce CAViAR (Causal Accident Video and Incident Analysis Repository), a human-annotated dashcam benchmark comprising 2,249 real-world accident videos collected from CarCrashDataset (CCD) and Nexar. Each video is annotated with structured labels spanning environmental conditions, accident type, causal explanation, apparent At-Fault Agent, affected agent, and apparent rule-violation category. We benchmark state-of-the-art vision-language models (VLMs), including Cosmos-Reason2, Qwen3-VL, and InternVL3. Once class imbalance is accounted for with majority/random baselines and balanced metrics, perceptual competence is uneven--lighting is nearly solved, whereas weather and road-condition accuracy fall at or below the majority-class baseline---and all models degrade sharply on accident type and responsibility reasoning. Overall, CAViAR exposes a practical Perception--Reasoning Gap: current VLMs may recognize salient context, but do not reliably map visible agent actions to annotated rule-relevant responsibility categories in safety-critical driving scenarios. Code, annotation schema, prompts, and evaluation scripts are available at: https://github.com/nec-labs-ma/CAViAR

AI.tldr: CAViAR is a new human-annotated benchmark of 2,249 real-world dashcam accident videos with structured labels (environment, accident type, causality, at-fault agent, affected agent, rule violation). Evaluation of state-of-the-art VLMs reveals a Perception–Reasoning Gap: models perform well on perceptual tasks like lighting but poorly on weather, road conditions, accident type, and responsibility reasoning.
AI.motivation: Modern autonomous driving systems excel at perception (detection, trajectory prediction) but lack high-level causal reasoning needed for accident interpretation, particularly determining fault and violated traffic rules—an area largely unexplored in current benchmarks.
AI.method: Created CAViAR by collecting 2,249 human-annotated accident videos from CarCrashDataset (CCD) and Nexar, with structured annotations covering environmental conditions, accident type, causal explanation, at-fault agent, affected agent, and rule-violation category. Benchmarked state-of-the-art VLMs (Cosmos-Reason2, Qwen3-VL, InternVL3) using balanced metrics and majority/random baselines to account for class imbalance.
AI.result: Perceptual competence is uneven: lighting classification is nearly solved, while weather and road-condition accuracy fall at or below majority-class baseline. All models degrade sharply on accident type and responsibility reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: CAViAR exposes a practical Perception–Reasoning Gap: current VLMs can recognize salient context but do not reliably map visible agent actions to rule-relevant responsibility categories in safety-critical driving scenarios. Benchmark resources are publicly released.

title: Beyond Recognition: Compact Multi-Domain Arabic Manuscript HTR with Candidate-Selection Analysis and Evidence-Preserving Review
summary: Historical Arabic manuscript transcription is not only a recognition problem. A usable scholarly system must cope with shifting hands and layouts, preserve uncertain readings, distinguish visual evidence from linguistic plausibility, and record the researcher's final decision. We present Phoenix, a 4.99-million-parameter CNN-BiLSTM-CTC recognizer, and Athar, an evidence-aware review workflow built around it. Phoenix is adapted across archival, Maghrebi, and historical manuscript domains using document-aware replay, an expanded 81-symbol codec, and forgetting guards that reject checkpoints that improve a new domain at unacceptable cost to previous domains. In a pre-specified held-out comparison against the preceding checkpoint, frozen before evaluation and scored with greedy decoding and raw references, Phoenix reduced CER from 22.12% to 17.86% on 10,594 Agapet lines and from 17.72% to 11.84% on 11,684 Omar lines, while regressing from 10.39% to 10.72% on 164 TariMa lines. Across the two large held-out sets, character-weighted CER fell from 19.98% to 14.93%, a 25.3% relative error reduction. A separate same-protocol development diagnostic found the lowest CER for Phoenix on four of four comparable domains (9.59% unweighted macro CER). An N-best diagnostic revealed a 2.15-point oracle gap between beam decoding and Oracle@25, while neural text rerankers, consensus MBR, CTC-posterior quality estimation, and local pre-CTC hidden-state quality estimation recovered less than 4% of this gap. Athar therefore preserves the visual reading, exposes bounded alternatives, uses local language models conservatively, retrieves source parallels with unique, ambiguous, or abstain states, and exports auditable TEI and PAGE-XML records. The results support evaluating manuscript HTR as auditable evidence management rather than silent text replacement.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Phoenix, a 4.99M-parameter CNN-BiLSTM-CTC recognizer for historical Arabic manuscripts, and Athar, an evidence-aware review workflow. Phoenix reduces CER from 19.98% to 14.93% (25.3% relative reduction) on held-out data while Athar preserves visual readings, exposes bounded alternatives, and exports auditable TEI/PAGE-XML records.
AI.motivation: Historical Arabic manuscript transcription is more than a recognition problem—it requires handling shifting hands and layouts, preserving uncertain readings, distinguishing visual evidence from linguistic plausibility, and recording researcher decisions. Existing systems fail to treat transcription as auditable evidence management.
AI.method: Phoenix uses a 4.99M-parameter CNN-BiLSTM-CTC architecture with document-aware replay, an expanded 81-symbol codec, and forgetting guards to prevent catastrophic forgetting. Athar is a review workflow preserving visual readings, exposing bounded alternatives, using local language models conservatively, retrieving source parallels with uncertainty states, and exporting auditable TEI/PAGE-XML records.
AI.result: Phoenix reduced CER from 22.12% to 17.86% on Agapet lines and from 17.72% to 11.84% on Omar lines, with minor regression on TariMa. Character-weighted CER fell from 19.98% to 14.93% (25.3% relative reduction). N-best diagnostics showed a 2.15-point oracle gap that rerankers and quality estimators recovered less than 4% of.
AI.conclusion: The results support evaluating manuscript HTR as auditable evidence management rather than silent text replacement, demonstrating that a system combining domain-adapted recognition with an evidence-aware review workflow is more suitable for scholarly use.

title: HiRA-CAM: Preserving Fine-Grained Spatial Relevance in Gradient-Based Visual Explanations
comment: IEEE World Congress on Computational Intelligence, Maastricht, Netherlands, June 2026
summary: Deep Learning models can include billions of parameters or more, making it difficult to explain their internal transformations and outputs. However, explainability is increasing in importance due to the use of AI in crucial applications. This paper focuses on the interpretability of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Building on the popular gradient based method LayerCAM for extracting internal features in CNNs, we propose an improved method named HiRA-CAM, and show that it outperforms both LayerCAM and Grad-CAM on creating useful saliency maps for object classification. The main feature of HiRA-CAM is its adaptive use of activation maps from all the layers of the CNN to arrive at a more focused saliency map.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes HiRA-CAM, an improved saliency map method for CNN interpretability that builds on LayerCAM and Grad-CAM by adaptively using activation maps from all CNN layers to produce more focused and useful saliency maps for object classification.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models are increasingly large (billions of parameters) and difficult to explain, yet explainability is critical for AI in important applications. Current gradient-based methods like Grad-CAM and LayerCAM have limitations in producing useful saliency maps for CNN interpretability.
AI.method: HiRA-CAM builds on LayerCAM and improves it by adaptively leveraging activation maps from all layers of the CNN, rather than only a subset, to generate more focused saliency maps for object classification.
AI.result: HiRA-CAM outperforms both LayerCAM and Grad-CAM in creating useful saliency maps for object classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: Adaptively combining activation maps across all CNN layers yields improved interpretability, making HiRA-CAM a more effective saliency map method than existing gradient-based approaches.

title: VideoRun2D Demo: Markerless Body Tracking for Biomechanical Analysis of Running
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. IEEE/CVF Conf. on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW), 2026 (1st PhysHuman Workshop: Physically Grounded Human Perception and Modeling)
summary: Human pose estimation has advanced significantly due to the development of deep learning models, increased data availability, and improved computing resources. These developments have led to highly accurate body tracking systems with direct applications in sports analysis and performance evaluation. The VideoRun2D Demo performs a biomechanical analysis during sprints using different human pose estimators. The proposed framework was evaluated using human pose trackers and expert manual annotations. The tested framework uses 314 sprints from 44 professional runners, focusing on two key joint angles in sprint biomechanics: 1) hip flexion/extension and 2) knee flexion/extension. The framework also includes a post-processing module for outlier detection. The tested results demonstrate that the average root-mean-square errors range from 11.46° to 5.83° for the best trackers. When integrated with the post-processing modules, these errors can be reduced to 9.87° and 5.30°, respectively. The VideoRun2D Demo findings suggest that human pose-tracking approaches can be valuable resources for the biomechanical analysis of running.

AI.tldr: The VideoRun2D Demo performs biomechanical analysis of sprints using human pose estimators, evaluating hip and knee joint angles across 314 sprints from 44 professional runners. The best trackers achieve average root-mean-square errors from 11.46° to 5.83°, which improve to 9.87° and 5.30° with post-processing outlier detection modules.
AI.motivation: To leverage advances in deep learning-based human pose estimation to provide an automated biomechanical analysis framework for running performance evaluation, reducing reliance on expert manual annotations.
AI.method: The framework evaluates multiple human pose trackers against expert manual annotations, focusing on hip and knee flexion/extension angles during sprints. It includes a post-processing module for outlier detection to refine joint angle estimates.
AI.result: Average root-mean-square errors range from 11.46° to 5.83° for the best trackers. With post-processing, errors are reduced to 9.87° and 5.30° respectively.
AI.conclusion: Human pose-tracking approaches can serve as valuable resources for biomechanical analysis of running, offering reasonably accurate automated joint angle estimation for sprint performance evaluation.

title: A Plug-in Interpretation of Conditioning in Score-Based Diffusion Models
summary: We propose a conditioning mechanism for diffusion models based on multi-speed joint diffusion of the target and the condition. The mechanism learns an unconditional joint score network and enforces conditioning at inference via a plug-in correction term. The plug-in term separates the conditioning contribution from the learned unconditional dynamics, offering a transparent view of how the condition steers generation of the target distribution. Building on this, we derive explicit conditional reverse-time SDEs and approximate probability-flow ODEs, enabling principled and directly comparable conditional samplers. To reduce the induced ODE--SDE discrepancy, we introduce a log-Fokker--Planck residual regularization that improves ODE sampling quality. Experiments on conditional image generation tasks demonstrate competitive performance and support the effectiveness of the plug-in conditioning view. Additional ODE--SDE comparison experiments show that the log-Fokker--Planck residual regularization improves deterministic ODE sampling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a plug-in conditioning mechanism for diffusion models based on multi-speed joint diffusion of the target and condition, using an unconditional joint score network with a plug-in correction term at inference. It derives explicit conditional reverse-time SDEs and approximate probability-flow ODEs, and introduces log-Fokker–Planck residual regularization to reduce ODE–SDE discrepancy.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion model conditioning mechanisms often lack transparency in how the condition steers generation and lack principled connections between SDE and ODE conditional sampling, motivating a more interpretable and theoretically grounded conditioning framework.
AI.method: The method uses multi-speed joint diffusion of the target and condition, trains an unconditional joint score network, and enforces conditioning at inference via a plug-in correction term that separates conditioning from the unconditional dynamics. Explicit conditional reverse-time SDEs and approximate probability-flow ODEs are derived, and a log-Fokker–Planck residual regularization is introduced to improve ODE sampling quality.
AI.result: Experiments on conditional image generation show competitive performance. ODE–SDE comparison experiments demonstrate that the log-Fokker–Planck residual regularization improves deterministic ODE sampling.
AI.conclusion: The plug-in conditioning view is effective and transparent, and the proposed regularization successfully bridges the gap between ODE and SDE sampling in conditional diffusion models.

title: CVSD-Reg: Cross-Modal Visual Semantic Prior Distillation for Robust LiDAR Registration
summary: Learning-based global point cloud registration has achieved remarkable progress, yet its reliance on geometric representations makes existing methods sensitive to variations in point density, scan pattern, viewpoint, and sensor characteristics. We propose CVSD-Reg, a robust global LiDAR registration framework that distills visual semantic priors from a vision foundation model into LiDAR representations. In Stage 1, a Point Transformer V3 student learns from a frozen DINOv2 teacher through contrastive distillation and spherical-manifold alignment, which preserves the hyperspherical geometry of the teacher embedding space. Self-supervised InfoNCE consistency and soft $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ invariance further encourage viewpoint-robust descriptors. In Stage 2, the distilled representation is adapted to registration through correspondence learning, density-aware point-dropout augmentation, and end-to-end pose optimization. With a single checkpoint, CVSD-Reg generalizes to both single-sensor and zero-shot cross-sensor scenarios without sensor-specific adaptation and remains entirely camera-free at inference. On KITTI, nuScenes, and HeLiPR, CVSD-Reg achieves strict success rate (SR@0.5\,m/$1^\circ$) of 97.7$\%$, 99.0$\%$, and 99.3$\%$, respectively, including 97.3$\%$ on sparse 16-beam Velodyne scans. It outperforms state-of-the-art geometric registration methods by up to 44.0 percentage points without requiring camera inputs or post-hoc ICP refinement.

AI.tldr: CVSD-Reg is a robust global LiDAR registration framework that distills visual semantic priors from a frozen DINOv2 vision foundation model into LiDAR point cloud representations via contrastive distillation and spherical-manifold alignment. It achieves state-of-the-art registration performance across KITTI, nuScenes, and HeLiPR benchmarks, including strong zero-shot cross-sensor generalization and robustness to sparse 16-beam scans, without requiring camera inputs at inference.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based global point cloud registration methods rely purely on geometric representations, making them sensitive to variations in point density, scan pattern, viewpoint, and sensor characteristics. The authors aim to overcome these limitations by leveraging visual semantic priors from a vision foundation model.
AI.method: The framework has two stages: (1) Distillation stage where a Point Transformer V3 student learns from a frozen DINOv2 teacher through contrastive distillation and spherical-manifold alignment, preserving hyperspherical geometry, with self-supervised InfoNCE consistency and soft SE(3) invariance for viewpoint robustness; (2) Registration stage where the distilled representation is adapted through correspondence learning, density-aware point-dropout augmentation, and end-to-end pose optimization. The method remains camera-free at inference and requires no sensor-specific adaptation.
AI.result: CVSD-Reg achieves strict success rates (SR@0.5m/1°) of 97.7% on KITTI, 99.0% on nuScenes, and 99.3% on HeLiPR, including 97.3% on sparse 16-beam Velodyne scans. It outperforms state-of-the-art geometric methods by up to 44.0 percentage points without camera inputs or ICP refinement.
AI.conclusion: Distilling visual semantic priors from vision foundation models into LiDAR representations significantly enhances the robustness and generalization of global point cloud registration, enabling a single checkpoint to handle both single-sensor and zero-shot cross-sensor scenarios effectively.

title: Where Grounding Accuracy Lives on the IoU Curve: Label-Free Inference-Time Boundary Refinement
summary: Vision--language models can identify the correct referent while returning an imprecise bounding box. We study whether a frozen direct-answer model can use its own prediction to allocate one additional localized observation without accessing target annotations at inference. Label-free precision refinement (LFPR) routes predicted-small regions to a higher-resolution pass, re-grounds the expression inside a context crop, admits a candidate only under fixed geometric guards, and returns a fixed coordinate-wise midpoint. We report results across three evidence tiers. On 31,921 retrospective Ref-L4 expressions, LFPR raises mAcc$_{0.5:0.95}$ from 72.947\% to 76.013\% (Acc@0.5 88.531\%$\to$89.725\%, Acc@0.9 55.788\%$\to$61.142\%). A frozen transfer to 30,969 RefCOCO/RefCOCO+/RefCOCOg expressions improves every dataset at Acc@0.5, mAcc, and mean IoU (pooled mAcc $+0.645$, Acc@0.5 $+0.817$), while Acc@0.9 is unchanged overall: routing alone gains $+1.162$ points there, but crop, guards, and fusion give back $-1.192$, offsetting rather than showing no strict-IoU effect. A prospective, image-disjoint Flickr30K Entities evaluation improves every endpoint (mAcc $+0.973$, Acc@0.9 $+1.022$), more strongly under a single-box variant (mAcc $+2.575$, Acc@0.9 $+3.689$). The same operator applied to two released grounding specialists improves every endpoint (Acc@0.9 $+1.569$/$+6.716$ for EGM-4B/8B) at roughly twice the latency, composing with specialist training rather than replacing it. A genuine unguarded control (guard removed from the same candidates) underperforms the incumbent on every metric, showing the guard is load-bearing. Together, these results show that referent selection and boundary precision are partially separable, with different components moving opposing regions of the IoU curve -- behavior a single threshold cannot reveal.

AI.tldr: LFPR is a label-free precision refinement method that lets a frozen direct-answer model use its own prediction to allocate one additional localized observation, improving grounding precision across multiple benchmarks and model types by routing predictions through higher-resolution passes with geometric guards.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models often identify the correct referent but return imprecise bounding boxes. The paper investigates whether a frozen model can use its own predictions to refine localization without needing target annotations at inference time.
AI.method: LFPR routes predicted-small regions to a higher-resolution pass, re-grounds the expression within a context crop, admits candidates only under fixed geometric guards, and returns a fixed coordinate-wise midpoint. It operates without accessing target annotations at inference.
AI.result: On Ref-L4, LFPR raises mAcc0.5:0.95 from 72.947% to 76.013%. Transfer to RefCOCO/RefCOCO+/RefCOCOg improves every dataset at Acc@0.5, mAcc, and mean IoU. Flickr30K Entities evaluation improves every endpoint with stronger gains under a single-box variant. Applying to grounding specialists (EGM-4B/8B) improves every endpoint at roughly twice latency. A control without the guard underperforms on all metrics.
AI.conclusion: Referent selection and boundary precision are partially separable, with different components moving opposing regions of the IoU curve—a behavior that a single threshold cannot reveal. LFPR composes with specialist training rather than replacing it.

title: Stream4D: 4D-Consistency for Streaming Autoregressive Diffusion Video Models
summary: Streaming autoregressive diffusion models enable real-time, long-horizon video generation, but their training objectives optimize local frame prediction rather than the geometry and dynamics of a coherent world: long rollouts accumulate geometric drift and degrade into static or unnatural motion. Recent bidirectional approaches address this problem using rewards signals built upon 3D Gaussian-Splatting reconstruction. However, a single rigid 3d reconstruction cannot model a dynamic scene, so this critic penalizes genuine object motion as reconstruction error and is maximized by freezing the video. This shortcut is especially detrimental in the AR setting, where each chunk can propagate an already-static configuration. In this work, we propose Stream4D, which replaces the static critic with a feed-forward 4D reconstruction reward that explicitly models scene dynamics, allowing coherent motion to receive high consistency rewards. To further guide motion magnitude and quality, we add a motion prior that rewards natural scene-flow magnitude while penalizing jitter and non-rigid artifacts. Our final recipe combines these two terms with a lightweight perceptual anchor. Across various autoregressive video backbones and various generation horizons, Stream4D improves 4D reconstruction quality, preserves motion more effectively, and achieves higher human-aligned preference. Project page: https://banyuanhao.github.io/Stream4D/

AI.tldr: Stream4D replaces static 3D critic with a feed-forward 4D reconstruction reward in streaming autoregressive diffusion models, using a motion prior to preserve coherent dynamics and reduce geometric drift in long-horizon video generation.
AI.motivation: Streaming autoregressive diffusion models suffer from geometric drift and degraded/static motion in long rollouts because their training objectives only optimize local frame prediction. Previous bidirectional approaches using 3D reconstruction rewards fail because a rigid 3D reconstruction cannot model dynamic scenes, penalizing genuine motion and encouraging frozen videos, which is especially damaging in autoregressive settings.
AI.method: Stream4D replaces the static 3D critic with a feed-forward 4D reconstruction reward that explicitly models scene dynamics, allowing coherent motion to receive high consistency rewards. It adds a motion prior that rewards natural scene-flow magnitude while penalizing jitter and non-rigid artifacts, combined with a lightweight perceptual anchor.
AI.result: Across various autoregressive video backbones and generation horizons, Stream4D improves 4D reconstruction quality, preserves motion more effectively, and achieves higher human-aligned preference.
AI.conclusion: Modeling scene dynamics explicitly via 4D reconstruction rewards, rather than rigid static reconstruction, is key to preventing geometric drift and motion degradation in streaming autoregressive video generation.

title: Block3D: Efficient Text-to-3D Generation via Block-Wise Diffusion
summary: While text-to-3D generation has advanced rapidly, achieving high geometric fidelity at low inference cost remains challenging. Existing text-to-3D methods either decode discrete shape tokens autoregressively or iteratively refine global 3D representations with diffusion or flow models. However, autoregressive decoding is sequential and cannot revise errors, whereas diffusion and flow-matching models repeatedly process the full representation, making high-quality generation increasingly expensive. In this paper, we propose Block3D, a block-wise diffusion framework that partitions the discrete shape-token sequence into contiguous blocks, generates the blocks autoregressively, and jointly denoises all tokens within the current block. To alleviate error accumulation, we introduce confidence-guided intra-block correction, which revises low-confidence tokens before each block is finalized. On a held-out set from TRELLIS-500K, Block3D reduces mean end-to-end generation time from 25.71 seconds to 4.99 seconds, achieving a $5.15\times$ speedup over the fine-tuned autoregressive baseline without sacrificing geometric fidelity.

AI.tldr: Block3D is a block-wise diffusion framework for text-to-3D generation that partitions discrete shape tokens into contiguous blocks, generates them autoregressively while jointly denoising tokens within each block. It includes confidence-guided intra-block correction to reduce error accumulation, achieving a 5.15× speedup (25.71s → 4.99s) over autoregressive baselines without sacrificing geometric fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-3D methods face a trade-off: autoregressive decoding is sequential and cannot revise errors, while diffusion/flow-matching models repeatedly process the full representation making high-quality generation expensive. The goal is to achieve high geometric fidelity at low inference cost.
AI.method: Block3D partitions the discrete shape-token sequence into contiguous blocks, generates blocks autoregressively, and jointly denoises all tokens within the current block. It introduces confidence-guided intra-block correction to revise low-confidence tokens before each block is finalized, mitigating error accumulation.
AI.result: On a held-out set from TRELLIS-500K, Block3D reduces mean end-to-end generation time from 25.71 seconds to 4.99 seconds, achieving a 5.15× speedup over the fine-tuned autoregressive baseline while maintaining geometric fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Block3D demonstrates that combining block-wise autoregressive generation with intra-block diffusion denoising offers an effective balance between generation speed and geometric fidelity, addressing the limitations of both pure autoregressive and full diffusion approaches.

title: Mix&Fix-Net: A Dual-Stage Trajectory Prediction Model for AIS and Vision-Derived Vessel Data
summary: Vessel trajectory prediction is critical for maritime safety and accident prevention. While most existing trajectory prediction models rely on Automatic Identification System (AIS) data due to its precision and availability, small vessels mostly operate without AIS, resulting in a significant monitoring gap. To address this, we propose Mix&Fix-Net, a dual-stage mixer-based trajectory prediction model designed to handle vessel trajectory time-series data derived from both AIS and (non-AIS) vision data. Our architecture integrates a Primary Trajectory Predictor with a Residual Trajectory Adjuster, enabling more refined trajectory prediction. Additionally, we introduce a new video-based dataset derived from webcam streams, from which vessel trajectories are extracted to represent non-AIS data. Extensive evaluations on both AIS and non-AIS datasets across six metrics (mean squared error, mean absolute error, symmetric mean absolute percentage error, final displacement error, Frechet distance, and average Euclidean distance) demonstrate that Mix&Fix-Net consistently outperforms existing baselines across most metrics and datasets.

AI.tldr: Mix&Fix-Net is a dual-stage mixer-based trajectory prediction model for vessels that handles both AIS and non-AIS (vision-derived) trajectory data, integrating a Primary Trajectory Predictor with a Residual Trajectory Adjuster, and introduces a new webcam-based video dataset for non-AIS vessel trajectories.
AI.motivation: Most vessel trajectory prediction models depend on AIS data, leaving small vessels that operate without AIS systems unmonitored — creating a significant gap in maritime safety and accident prevention coverage.
AI.method: Mix&Fix-Net uses a dual-stage architecture comprising a Primary Trajectory Predictor and a Residual Trajectory Adjuster, built on mixer-based designs to process trajectory time-series from both AIS and vision-derived data. A new webcam-based video dataset with extracted vessel trajectories is also introduced to represent non-AIS data.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on AIS and non-AIS datasets across six metrics (MSE, MAE, SMAPE, FDE, Frechet distance, and average Euclidean distance) show Mix&Fix-Net consistently outperforms existing baselines across most metrics and datasets.
AI.conclusion: Mix&Fix-Net effectively addresses the non-AIS vessel trajectory prediction gap by providing robust performance on both data types, with the dual-stage refinement approach proving superior to existing baselines.

title: VGI-BENCH: Probing Visual Intelligence in Video Generation Models
summary: Recent studies suggest that video generation models can exhibit certain forms of zero-shot visual reasoning through generated frames. Yet reliable evaluation remains challenging: benchmarks should adopt inputs aligned with the visual priors of current video models, require valid evolving processes rather than only plausible final states, and calibrate task difficulty to remain challenging yet partly feasible. To this end, we introduce VGI-bench, containing 27 tasks and 810 instances, organized by a two-level taxonomy of task domains and skill tags for fine-grained evaluation of visual reasoning capabilities of video generation models. Our evaluations show that current generative systems can solve a subset of visually grounded reasoning tasks, but remain far from reliable, with even the strongest model, Seedance~2.0, achieving only 51.0% under our evaluation criteria. Our analysis further explore the output failure modes, input condition sensitivity, performance transfer boundary from synthetic fine-tuning, and internal denoising perspective revealing limited self-correction, where later steps mainly refine early hypotheses rather than correct reasoning errors. We hope VGI-bench will help stimulate the development of next-generation video generation models. We will release our code and data.

AI.tldr: VGI-bench is a new benchmark with 27 tasks and 810 instances for evaluating visual reasoning in video generation models, finding that current models (best: Seedance 2.0 at 51.0%) can solve some tasks but remain unreliable. The benchmark includes a two-level taxonomy and reveals failure modes, input sensitivity, and limited self-correction in denoising.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for evaluating video generation models' visual reasoning capabilities are unreliable because they fail to align with models' visual priors, don't require valid evolving processes, and don't calibrate task difficulty properly.
AI.method: Introduces VGI-bench with 27 tasks and 810 instances organized by a two-level taxonomy of task domains and skill tags, along with evaluation criteria for visual reasoning in video generation.
AI.result: Current generative systems solve a subset of visually grounded reasoning tasks but remain far from reliable; the strongest model (Seedance 2.0) achieves only 51.0%. Analysis reveals output failure modes, input condition sensitivity, limited performance transfer from synthetic fine-tuning, and limited self-correction in the denoising process.
AI.conclusion: VGI-bench aims to stimulate development of next-generation video generation models; code and data will be released.

title: PEA-DPO: Perception-Enhanced Alignment Direct Preference Optimization for MLLMs Alignment
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has emerged as an effective approach for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, its adaptation to multimodal settings remains unexplored. Through representational analysis, we identify a key limitation in multimodal preference optimization, which we term visual insensitivity: models often fail to distinguish between images and those with critical visual context removed. Our theoretical analysis further uncovers two manifestations of this problem, namely Across-Image Insensitivity and Within-Image Insensitivity. To address these challenges, we propose Perception-Enhanced Alignment DPO (PEA-DPO), a framework for multimodal LLMs alignment, which explicitly leverages visual preference signals to overcome visual insensitivity. We further provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that PEA-DPO provably mitigates both failure modes. Empirical results demonstrate that PEA-DPO enhances sensitivity to visual context while preserving the language modeling capacity of the base model. Evaluations across three hallucination benchmarks using MLLMs of varying scales show that PEA-DPO effectively mitigates visual insensitivity, achieves stronger multimodal alignment, and substantially reduces hallucinations.

AI.tldr: PEA-DPO is a framework that extends Direct Preference Optimization to multimodal settings by explicitly leveraging visual preference signals, addressing the visual insensitivity problem in multimodal LLMs—where models fail to distinguish images with critical visual context removed—and provably mitigating both Across-Image and Within-Image insensitivity, reducing hallucinations across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: DPO is effective for aligning LLMs with human preferences but has not been adapted to multimodal settings. Through representational analysis, the authors identify a key limitation called "visual insensitivity," where multimodal models fail to distinguish between original images and those with critical visual context removed. This problem manifests as two failure modes: Across-Image and Within-Image insensitivity.
AI.method: The paper proposes Perception-Enhanced Alignment DPO (PEA-DPO), a framework that explicitly leverages visual preference signals to overcome visual insensitivity in multimodal LLM alignment. The authors also provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that PEA-DPO provably mitigates both Across-Image and Within-Image insensitivity failure modes.
AI.result: Empirical results show PEA-DPO enhances sensitivity to visual context while preserving the language modeling capacity of the base model. Evaluations across three hallucination benchmarks using MLLMs of varying scales demonstrate that PEA-DPO effectively mitigates visual insensitivity, achieves stronger multimodal alignment, and substantially reduces hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: PEA-DPO provides an effective solution for multimodal preference alignment that overcomes the visual insensitivity limitation inherent in standard DPO, provably addressing both failure modes and significantly reducing hallucinations in multimodal LLMs while maintaining language modeling performance.

title: TextRefine: Improving Textual Fidelity, Spatial Placement, and Glyph Rendering for Text Editing in Product Posters
summary: Text editing in product posters entails inserting new text or replacing existing text while preserving product appearance, background content, and global composition. Despite recent progress in instruction-based image editing, general-purpose models remain unreliable in this setting: they often omit or incorrectly render the target text, place it over salient products or pre-existing content, and produce structurally distorted or visually inconsistent glyphs. We introduce \textbf{TextRefine}, a task-aligned post-training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning with operation-specific reward optimization to address these complementary failure modes. For text insertion, our text-span-level reward jointly assesses semantic fidelity and target-span coverage, penalizes spatial conflicts with products and existing text, and employs a gated structural constraint to preserve non-text regions. For text replacement, our glyph-level reward leverages the connectionist temporal classification (CTC) posterior of the target character to provide graded supervision for fine-grained defects, including missing strokes, structural deformations, and confusion among visually similar characters. We further introduce \textbf{OpenTextEdit}, a dataset comprising 100K images for text editing in product posters, with multi-text layouts, detailed text attributes, product masks, and challenging low-frequency characters. Extensive experiments on both insertion and replacement demonstrate that TextRefine consistently outperforms the evaluated image editing baselines in textual fidelity, placement reliability, and glyph quality while better preserving source-image content.

AI.tldr: TextRefine is a task-aligned post-training framework for text editing in product posters, combining supervised fine-tuning with operation-specific reward optimization (text-span-level rewards for insertion, glyph-level CTC-based rewards for replacement), together with OpenTextEdit, a 100K-image dataset for this task.
AI.motivation: General-purpose instruction-based image editing models fail at text editing in product posters due to omitted/incorrect target text, text placed over salient content, and structurally distorted glyphs.
AI.method: A two-component framework: (1) supervised fine-tuning aligned to the task, plus (2) operation-specific reward optimization—text-span-level rewards for insertion (semantic fidelity, span coverage, spatial conflict penalties, gated structural constraints) and glyph-level CTC posterior rewards for replacement (graded supervision for missing strokes, deformations, and similar-character confusion). Also introduces OpenTextEdit dataset with 100K images.
AI.result: TextRefine consistently outperforms existing image editing baselines on both text insertion and replacement across textual fidelity, placement reliability, and glyph quality, while better preserving source-image content.
AI.conclusion: Task-aligned post-training with operation-specific rewards effectively addresses complementary failure modes in poster text editing, and the OpenTextEdit dataset enables training and evaluation for this specialized setting.

title: S$^2$GS: Structured Sparse Gaussian Streaming for Efficient Free-Viewpoint Video Reconstruction on Edge-IoT Devices
comment: Project Page, Code, and Supplementary Material: https://github.com/liyw420/S2GS
summary: Streaming reconstruction of Free-Viewpoint Videos (FVVs) supports immersive Internet of Things (IoT) services, such as telepresence and digital twin visualization. Existing methods suffer from high per-frame optimization time and large storage footprints, limiting deployment on resource-constrained Edge-IoT devices. To address these challenges, we propose Structured Sparse Gaussian Streaming (S$^2$GS), an FVV reconstruction framework that exploits structure-aware temporal sparsity to selectively update Gaussian residuals, enabling efficient streaming without compromising visual fidelity. In the spatial domain, a streaming octree hierarchically organizes Gaussian residuals, capturing spatial correlations that guide residual updates. In the temporal domain, a structured gating mechanism, comprising hierarchical feature propagation (HFP) and Gumbel-Sigmoid sampling, converts hierarchical dynamic cues into sparse residual update decisions under differentiable optimization. A multi-level discrete scheme is further adopted to provide fine-grained control over residual updates while preserving intricate dynamic details. Extensive experiments across consumer GPUs, industrial edge IoT devices, and a physical telepresence testbed demonstrate that S$^2$GS consistently reduces per-frame optimization time and storage footprint while maintaining competitive visual quality. Compared with QUEEN, S$^2$GS reduces per-frame optimization time by 59% and storage costs by 85% on an RTX 4090 GPU. On the Jetson AGX Orin, S$^2$GS delivers the highest rendering throughput (60+ FPS) and the lowest energy consumption among the evaluated methods, demonstrating its potential for deployment in resource-constrained systems.

AI.tldr: S^2GS is a streaming Free-Viewpoint Video reconstruction framework that exploits structure-aware temporal sparsity (via streaming octree and structured gating with Gumbel-Sigmoid sampling) to selectively update Gaussian residuals, reducing per-frame optimization time by 59% and storage costs by 85% while maintaining visual quality, and achieving 60+ FPS on edge IoT devices.
AI.motivation: Existing FVV reconstruction methods suffer from high per-frame optimization time and large storage footprints, limiting deployment on resource-constrained Edge-IoT devices for immersive services like telepresence and digital twin visualization.
AI.method: S^2GS exploits structure-aware temporal sparsity: (1) spatially, a streaming octree hierarchically organizes Gaussian residuals to capture spatial correlations guiding updates; (2) temporally, a structured gating mechanism with hierarchical feature propagation (HFP) and Gumbel-Sigmoid sampling converts hierarchical dynamic cues into sparse residual update decisions; (3) a multi-level discrete scheme provides fine-grained control over residual updates.
AI.result: Compared with QUEEN, S^2GS reduces per-frame optimization time by 59% and storage costs by 85% on RTX 4090. On Jetson AGX Orin, it achieves the highest rendering throughput (60+ FPS) and lowest energy consumption among evaluated methods.
AI.conclusion: S^2GS demonstrates efficient FVV streaming reconstruction with lower computational and storage overhead while maintaining competitive visual quality, showing strong potential for deployment on resource-constrained Edge-IoT systems.

title: When Guidance Goes Off-Scale: Recalibrating Diffusion Transformers under Analog Compute-in-Memory Nonidealities
summary: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) incur high memory traffic and energy costs because sampling repeatedly evaluates large denoisers dominated by linear operations. Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) can alleviate these costs by executing linear operations within weight-storing memory arrays. However, CIM nonidealities perturb effective weights, with errors accumulating along the state-dependent denoising trajectory; their interaction with classifier-free guidance (CFG) remains underexplored. In this paper, we characterize the impact of analog CIM nonidealities on DiT sampling. Although conditional and unconditional predictions can each remain close to their clean counterparts, their difference (the CFG residual) is disproportionately attenuated and rotated. Identifying this residual as a controllable failure channel, we propose a retraining-free, sampler-side recalibration that adjusts only the CFG scale for a given CIM condition. Trajectory-level analysis shows that moderate recalibration strengthens the target-oriented component preserved in the distorted residual, enabling earlier commitment to a prompt-consistent semantic region. In contrast, excessive guidance amplifies the full noisy residual and degrades quality, resulting in a finite, noise-dependent optimum. Extensive experiments on PixArt-Sigma, PixArt-alpha, and DiT-XL/2 show that the optimal guidance scale increases with CIM noise. Using 30,000 samples per condition, guidance recalibration consistently restores generation quality across simulated CIM mappings, closing at least 87% of the CIM-induced FID gap at a CIM noise level of 0.20. It reduces FID from 59.22 to 20.49 on PixArt-Sigma, 72.37 to 21.12 on PixArt-alpha, and 20.89 to 6.62 on DiT-XL/2.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes the impact of analog compute-in-memory (CIM) nonidealities on Diffusion Transformer (DiT) sampling, identifying the classifier-free guidance (CFG) residual as a controllable failure channel. The authors propose a retraining-free, sampler-side recalibration that adjusts only the CFG scale for a given CIM condition, restoring generation quality by closing at least 87% of the CIM-induced FID gap across three model architectures.
AI.motivation: DiTs incur high memory traffic and energy costs during sampling due to repeated evaluation of large denoisers dominated by linear operations. Analog CIM can alleviate these costs, but CIM nonidealities perturb effective weights and cause errors that accumulate along the denoising trajectory. The interaction between these nonidealities and classifier-free guidance is not well understood.
AI.method: The authors characterize how analog CIM nonidealities affect DiT sampling, showing that the CFG residual (difference between conditional and unconditional predictions) is disproportionately attenuated and rotated even when individual predictions remain close to their clean counterparts. They propose a retraining-free, sampler-side recalibration that adjusts only the CFG scale given a specific CIM condition, based on trajectory-level analysis of the distorted residual.
AI.result: Experiments on PixArt-Sigma, PixArt-alpha, and DiT-XL/2 show that the optimal guidance scale increases with CIM noise. Using 30,000 samples per condition, guidance recalibration consistently restores generation quality, closing at least 87% of the CIM-induced FID gap at CIM noise level 0.20. FID is reduced from 59.22 to 20.49 on PixArt-Sigma, 72.37 to 21.12 on PixArt-alpha, and 20.89 to 6.62 on DiT-XL/2.
AI.conclusion: Moderate recalibration of CFG strengthens the target-oriented component preserved in the distorted residual, enabling earlier commitment to a prompt-consistent semantic region, while excessive guidance amplifies the full noisy residual and degrades quality, resulting in a finite, noise-dependent optimum. This makes CFG recalibration an effective, retraining-free mitigation strategy for CIM-induced errors in DiT sampling.

title: PL-NBA: A Possession-level Universal Basketball Video Dataset Supporting Multiple Visual Understanding Tasks
summary: Visual understanding in sports has emerged as a hot topic in computer vision in recent years. Most existing basketball video datasets adopt single action or activity as sample, which can neither preserve the temporal continuity of game events nor support complex tasks such as action anticipation. To address this issue, this paper constructs the first possession-level basketball video dataset (PL-NBA), in which each sample is composed of a complete NBA offensive possession. Collected from 60 NBA games, PL-NBA contains 11,000 valid offensive possession clips and 31,567 annotated events with player names, captions, event types and timestamps. Each video clip includes multiple events and preserves the continuity of events, which is helpful for analysis of tactic. Experiment is conducted on multiple visual understanding tasks, including event recognition, video captioning, temporal action localization and action anticipation. Experimental results show that existing methods achieve limited performance on above four tasks, demonstrating that PL-NBA is a challenging benchmark for sports video understanding.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces PL-NBA, the first possession-level basketball video dataset containing 11,000 offensive possession clips from 60 NBA games with 31,567 annotated events. Existing methods perform poorly on this benchmark across four visual understanding tasks, demonstrating its challenge.
AI.motivation: Most existing basketball video datasets use single actions or activities as samples, which cannot preserve temporal continuity of game events or support complex tasks like action anticipation. A possession-level dataset is needed to capture the full context of game events.
AI.method: The authors construct PL-NBA by collecting data from 60 NBA games, creating 11,000 valid offensive possession clips with 31,567 annotated events including player names, captions, event types, and timestamps. Each clip contains multiple events preserving temporal continuity.
AI.result: Experiments across four tasks (event recognition, video captioning, temporal action localization, and action anticipation) show that existing methods achieve limited performance, indicating PL-NBA is a challenging benchmark for sports video understanding.
AI.conclusion: PL-NBA provides a more comprehensive and temporally continuous basketball video dataset that enables complex tasks such as action anticipation, setting a new challenging benchmark for the field.

title: MUST-PET: MUltimodal Self-supervised learning across Tracers for whole-body PET/CT-based lesion segmentation
summary: Deep learning-based whole-body PET-CT lesion segmentation can support cancer staging, treatment planning, and response assessment, but generalization is limited by scarce annotations and domain shifts. Self-supervised learning (SSL) can address these challenges but remains underexplored in pan-cancer, multi-tracer PET-CT. In this work, we propose MUST-PET (MUltimodal Self-Supervised learning across Tracers), a multimodal, multi-tracer SSL framework for generalizable whole-body PET-CT lesion segmentation. MUST-PET is trained and validated on a diverse, multi-institutional collection of pan-cancer PET-CT scans acquired with FDG and prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiotracers. MUST-PET uses context-aware masked reconstruction, where one modality is partially masked and reconstructed using complementary information from both PET and CT. The pretrained model is subsequently fine-tuned with labeled samples and evaluated for reconstruction quality, lesion segmentation, label efficiency, and generalizability across independent held-out datasets. MUST-PET reduces reconstruction error, improves lesion segmentation over training from scratch, and performs well with limited labeled data and on unseen external datasets, demonstrating the potential of multi-tracer SSL for label-efficient, generalizable whole-body PET-CT. segmentation.

AI.tldr: MUST-PET is a multimodal, multi-tracer self-supervised learning framework for whole-body PET-CT lesion segmentation that uses context-aware masked reconstruction to pretrain on diverse pan-cancer FDG and PSMA PET-CT scans, improving segmentation performance, label efficiency, and generalization to unseen datasets.
AI.motivation: Whole-body PET-CT lesion segmentation is clinically valuable for cancer staging and treatment assessment, but is limited by scarce annotations and domain shifts across different tracers and institutions. Self-supervised learning offers a promising solution but has been underexplored in pan-cancer, multi-tracer PET-CT settings.
AI.method: MUST-PET employs a multimodal SSL framework where one modality is partially masked and reconstructed using complementary information from both PET and CT (context-aware masked reconstruction). The model is pretrained on a diverse multi-institutional pan-cancer dataset with FDG and PSMA tracers, then fine-tuned on labeled data for lesion segmentation.
AI.result: MUST-PET reduces reconstruction error, improves lesion segmentation over training from scratch, performs well with limited labeled data, and generalizes effectively to unseen external datasets.
AI.conclusion: Multi-tracer self-supervised learning demonstrates strong potential for label-efficient and generalizable whole-body PET-CT lesion segmentation, addressing annotation scarcity and domain shift challenges in clinical cancer imaging.

title: Scaffolding Minds: Optimizing Latent Visual Target Representations for Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Latent reasoning has advanced multimodal reasoning through a two-stage training paradigm: (1) a helper image is encoded into latent tokens to teach visual chain-of-thought during a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage, and (2) these latent tokens are further refined with reward feedback during a reinforcement learning (RL) stage. In this paper, we identify two key limitations of this framework, one in each stage. First, the SFT stage typically relies on an off-the-shelf vision encoder to encode the helper image, yielding suboptimal latent representations that may not be well aligned with the downstream reasoning task. Second, existing RL methods treat the latent component only through deterministic regularization, which constrains policy drift but does not create alternative latent trajectories for exploration. To address these limitations, we propose Scaffolding Minds. Our approach learns a dedicated scaffolding encoder that provides an optimized target in latent space, and learns both the mean and variance of the RL sampler. We further show that these two improvements are complementary, together yielding substantial gains over strong baselines. Empirically, our method improves over the strongest latent-reasoning baseline by +9.5% on FrozenLake spatial planning, with the gain widening to +19% at 32x32 grid map, and by +5.2% on average across nine visual-centric reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies two limitations in the two-stage latent reasoning paradigm for multimodal reasoning: (1) SFT stage uses off-the-shelf vision encoders yielding suboptimal latent representations, and (2) RL stage uses only deterministic regularization that lacks exploration. They propose Scaffolding Minds, which learns a dedicated scaffolding encoder for optimized latent targets and learns both mean and variance of the RL sampler, achieving significant gains over strong baselines.
AI.motivation: The two-stage latent reasoning framework (SFT with helper image latent encoding followed by RL refinement) has two key weaknesses: the SFT stage relies on off-the-shelf vision encoders that produce suboptimal latent representations poorly aligned with downstream reasoning tasks, and the RL stage uses only deterministic regularization that constrains policy drift without enabling exploration of alternative latent trajectories.
AI.method: The proposed Scaffolding Minds approach: (1) learns a dedicated scaffolding encoder that provides an optimized target in latent space during the SFT stage, and (2) learns both the mean and variance of the RL sampler to enable stochastic exploration in latent space rather than only deterministic regularization.
AI.result: The method improves over the strongest latent-reasoning baseline by +9.5% on FrozenLake spatial planning, widening to +19% at 32x32 grid maps, and +5.2% on average across nine visual-centric reasoning benchmarks. The two improvements are shown to be complementary.
AI.conclusion: Scaffolding Minds demonstrates that both improving the latent representation quality in SFT via a dedicated scaffolding encoder and enabling stochastic exploration in RL via learning variance jointly contribute to substantial gains in multimodal latent reasoning performance.

title: RIPE++: Reinforced Keypoint Learning from Positive Pairs Only
summary: Sparse keypoint extraction and matching underpin core tasks in geometric computer vision, including structure-from-motion, visual SLAM, augmented reality, and medical image registration. Learning robust local feature representations, however, typically requires accurate camera poses or depth supervision, which are often unavailable in real-world settings. Reinforcement learning (RL) has recently emerged as a promising alternative, requiring only the information if two images show the same scene or not. However, existing RL formulations such as RIPE rely on coarse binary rewards and carefully constructed negative training pairs, limiting training stability and descriptor discriminability. In this paper, we revisit RL-based keypoint learning and propose a reward that fully exploits the geometric consistency signal, deriving both reward and penalty from a single positive pair without contrasting against negatives. This richer signal provides sufficient supervisory contrast to learn discriminative detectors and descriptors from positive image pairs alone, enabling representation learning under extremely limited supervision. Furthermore, we show that the same RL objective can be extended to the matching stage by adapting LightGlue, raising AUC@5 on MegaDepth1500 from 56.58 to 59.65 and enabling weakly-supervised training of the full sparse matching pipeline from image pairs with partial visual overlap. We validate our approach on established benchmarks, demonstrating competitive results compared to fully-supervised methods. We further show that the method can be even trained on low texture medical video sequences, where camera poses are usually unavailable and standard SfM pipelines often fail. Code and data are available at https://github.com/fraunhoferhhi/RIPEpp .

AI.tldr: This paper proposes RIPE++, an improved reinforcement learning-based approach for sparse keypoint extraction and matching that derives both reward and penalty from a single positive image pair, eliminating the need for negative pairs and enabling weakly-supervised training of the full sparse matching pipeline.
AI.motivation: Learning robust local features typically requires accurate camera poses or depth supervision, which are often unavailable in real-world settings. Existing RL formulations like RIPE rely on coarse binary rewards and carefully constructed negative training pairs, which limits training stability and descriptor discriminability.
AI.method: The approach revisits RL-based keypoint learning and proposes a reward that fully exploits geometric consistency signal, deriving both reward and penalty from a single positive pair without contrasting against negatives. This richer signal provides sufficient supervisory contrast for discriminative detector and descriptor learning from positive pairs alone. The same RL objective is extended to the matching stage by adapting LightGlue.
AI.result: The method raises AUC@5 on MegaDepth1500 from 56.58 to 59.65 and enables weakly-supervised training of the full sparse matching pipeline from image pairs with partial visual overlap. It demonstrates competitive results compared to fully-supervised methods on established benchmarks and can be trained on low-texture medical video sequences where camera poses are unavailable and standard SfM pipelines fail.
AI.conclusion: The proposed RL objective enables representation learning under extremely limited supervision with only positive image pair information, achieving competitive results against fully-supervised approaches and extending applicability to domains like medical imaging where pose supervision is unavailable.

title: Robust Cross-Modal Foundation Model Perception for Underwater Robots under Degraded Visual Conditions
summary: Reliable underwater robotic perception remains difficult because optical imagery degrades under turbidity, wavelength-dependent attenuation, low illumination, scattering, and blur. Although sonar provides complementary information that is less affected by optical visibility, prior visual-sonar research has largely focused on feature alignment and nominal detection performance. We investigate cross-modal robustness as visual reliability deteriorates and assess whether pretrained visual foundation-model representations can be complemented by sonar under severe degradation. We use frozen DINOv2 as the visual encoder and construct a controlled five-level benchmark ranging from clean to extreme visual conditions. We compare conventional visual detection, frozen foundation-model representations, sonar context, fixed multimodal fusion, clean-trained adaptive gating, and degradation-aware gated fusion. Our method trains the fusion mechanism across the full range of degradation while keeping the visual and sonar encoders frozen, allowing modality contributions to adapt without fine-tuning the pretrained backbone. Under extreme combined degradation, the DINOv2 baseline achieves 0.4610 balanced accuracy, while degradation-aware visual-sonar fusion reaches 0.6152, a 33.5% relative improvement. The learned sonar contribution increases from 14.2% under clean conditions to 41.3% under extreme degradation, demonstrating adaptive redistribution of cross-modal reliance. Fusion provides the largest gains under severe turbidity and blur, whereas color attenuation alone yields little additional benefit. These results show that foundation-model representations remain valuable but insufficient under severe information loss, and that explicitly adapting fusion to modality reliability can improve robust underwater multimodal perception.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates cross-modal robustness in underwater perception by combining frozen DINOv2 visual representations with sonar under controlled degradation levels. The proposed degradation-aware gated fusion achieves 33.5% relative improvement over DINOv2 baseline in extreme conditions, with learned sonar contribution increasing from 14.2% to 41.3% as visual quality deteriorates.
AI.motivation: Underwater optical imagery degrades severely under turbidity, attenuation, low illumination, and blur, yet prior visual-sonar research focused on feature alignment and nominal detection rather than robustness. The authors aim to assess whether pretrained visual foundation-model representations can be complemented by sonar under severe visual degradation.
AI.method: Frozen DINOv2 serves as the visual encoder with a controlled five-level benchmark from clean to extreme conditions. The method compares conventional detection, frozen foundation representations, sonar context, fixed fusion, clean-trained adaptive gating, and degradation-aware gated fusion. The fusion mechanism is trained across full degradation range while visual and sonar encoders remain frozen, enabling adaptive modality contribution without backbone fine-tuning.
AI.result: Under extreme combined degradation, DINOv2 baseline achieves 0.4610 balanced accuracy while degradation-aware visual-sonar fusion reaches 0.6152 (33.5% relative improvement). Sonar contribution grows from 14.2% (clean) to 41.3% (extreme). Largest gains occur under severe turbidity and blur; color attenuation alone provides little benefit.
AI.conclusion: Foundation-model visual representations remain valuable but insufficient under severe information loss. Explicitly adapting fusion to modality reliability improves robust underwater multimodal perception, demonstrating the value of degradation-aware cross-modal gating over fixed fusion strategies.

title: Scale-Separated Conditioning for Style-Encoder-Free Diffusion Stylization
summary: Reference-based diffusion stylization requires separating target geometry from transferable appearance. Existing tuning-based methods often rely on aligned content-style-target triplets or auxiliary visual encoders, which increases data cost and can transfer unintended scene structure from the style reference. We propose SEFS (Style-Encoder-Free Stylization), a style-encoder-free conditioning framework for diffusion transformers. SEFS forms style tokens from stochastic low-resolution crops of single training images. This crop bottleneck preserves local appearance statistics such as palette, stroke, texture, and material, while reducing access to global layout cues. Target content is encoded by edge and segmentation cues and fused with the noisy latent through parameter-efficient trainable projections. We add style-to-denoising re-normalization for token-statistic alignment and cross-block skip fusion for spatial detail. SEFS trains on unpaired single images; the frozen diffusion VAE is used only to place image conditions in the latent space. On artistic stylization benchmarks, SEFS improves content consistency and leakage diagnostics while retaining reference-style affinity, and ablations support the crop-resolution, re-normalization, and skip-fusion choices. The code of SEFS will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: SEFS is a style-encoder-free conditioning framework for diffusion transformers that stylizes images by extracting style tokens from stochastic low-resolution crops of a single training image, preserving local appearance (palette, stroke, texture, material) while avoiding global layout leakage. It fuses target content via edge/segmentation cues with the noisy latent using parameter-efficient projections, and adds style-to-denoising re-normalization and cross-block skip fusion. SEFS trains on unpaired single images and improves content consistency and leakage diagnostics on artistic stylization benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing reference-based diffusion stylization methods rely on tuning-based approaches that require aligned triplets or auxiliary encoders, increasing data costs and risking unintended transfer of scene structure from the style reference. The goal is to separate target geometry from transferable appearance without these dependencies.
AI.method: SEFS forms style tokens from stochastic low-resolution crops of single training images, using the crop bottleneck to preserve local appearance statistics while reducing global layout access. Target content is encoded via edge and segmentation cues, fused with the noisy latent through parameter-efficient trainable projections. Style-to-denoising re-normalization aligns token statistics, and cross-block skip fusion enhances spatial detail. The frozen diffusion VAE places image conditions in latent space, and training uses unpaired single images with no auxiliary visual encoder.
AI.result: On artistic stylization benchmarks, SEFS improves content consistency and leakage diagnostics while retaining reference-style affinity. Ablations confirm the effectiveness of crop-resolution, re-normalization, and skip-fusion design choices.
AI.conclusion: SEFS demonstrates that style-encoder-free conditioning with a crop bottleneck can effectively separate style from content in diffusion transformers, reducing data cost and leakage while maintaining style fidelity. The code will be publicly released.

title: StreamSoccer: Event-Driven Memory for Streaming Soccer Commentary
summary: Streaming video understanding requires models to causally update state as video arrives and organize growing history into semantic units that can evolve, persist, and be recalled under bounded computation and memory. This challenge is pronounced in live soccer commentary, where a system must describe completed events, summarize recent play, recall earlier events, or remain silent using only information available before each utterance. We present StreamSoccer, an event-driven system that uses event memory as its intermediate representation. A fixed-budget active memory integrates the stream; completed event states are retained locally and consolidated into retrievable historical records. A unified generator uses current, recent, and historical context to produce three commentary modes, while a rule-assisted scheduler selects a mode or silence. Unlike streaming video-language models organized around frames, visual tokens, or caches, and soccer-commentary methods based on predefined clips or output timestamps, StreamSoccer explicitly models event lifecycles. We construct a three-track streaming soccer commentary dataset and a layered evaluation protocol. At common reference anchors, StreamSoccer obtains CIDEr scores of 38.62, 23.96, and 17.39 for current-event, recent-window, and historical-memory commentary, ranking first on the current-event and historical-memory tracks and second on recent-window. Controlled ablations show that local completed events improve all tracks and that the full system performs best on all three. Across 174 raw-video runs on 58 matches, per-minute RTF p95 ranges from 0.10 to 0.22 without sustained growth with match history. These results indicate that event memory supports streaming soccer commentary across temporal scopes while controlling long-history computation.

AI.tldr: StreamSoccer is an event-driven streaming soccer commentary system that uses event memory as an intermediate representation, with a fixed-budget active memory, rule-assisted mode scheduling, and multi-scale context generation.
